evidence.text: A documented grave context securely locates the vessel; the owner’s identity is a more tentative inference.

production.text: Hand-forming, polishing and controlled firing produced a thin-walled vessel with contrasting surfaces.

material-work.text: Controlled forming, finishing and firing belonged to a wider urban setting of craft, household provision and institutions. Workshop location, imported objects and a distinctive ceramic style require different evidence for organization and identity.

name: Kerma, Egypt and a traveling beaker
place: Upper Nubia; selected beaker found at Abydos in Egypt
geographicPrecision: Kerma regional anchor; the actual beaker findspot is Abydos, separately stated.

interval.label: c. 2050–1500 BCE
interval.note: Middle and Classical Kerma frame in the regional chronology; not the full history of Nubia.

question: Can a pot identify the person buried beside it?
summary: A carefully finished beaker opens a wider inquiry into Nubian production, households and institutions. At Kerma, excavated craft installations and residential spaces place skilled work beside government and worship. This particular vessel was found at Abydos in Egypt; its documented context and the proposed identity of its owner remain different questions.

sections.title: Skilled hands controlled contrasting surfaces
sections.text: The beaker’s dark upper surface and red body began with choices about clay, finishing and fire. The Met describes hand-forming, red ocher and polishing before firing. Inverting vessels in combustible material helped create reducing conditions for the black top and interior. These were connected operations that makers had to manage. The irregular boundary is visible in the photograph; the proposed coating and firing explanation come from the catalogue, rather than being established by color alone.

sections.title: A capital organized different kinds of work
sections.text: Kerma was an independent Nubian capital with institutions beyond pottery production. Excavators identified residential quarters, royal buildings, administrative spaces, a circular audience hall and chapels around the principal temple. Craft installations occurred in several areas, especially near places of worship. Metalworking, faience and ceramics belonged to this setting. Placing those activities together shows how making, meeting and religious practice occupied an organized city; it does not establish that a king personally directed every workshop or that every worker had the same status.

citations.locator: La ville antique de Kerma: urban buildings and workshops

sections.title: Provisioning linked homes with the surrounding land
sections.text: The project’s residential account describes buildings arranged around courtyards, with kitchens, silos and other domestic annexes. Storing supplies and preparing meals gave household work a place in the city’s fabric. The broader livelihood account includes herding, plant resources, hunting and fishing. This setting helps explain why a finished vessel belongs in a history of production and provision, alongside the monumental buildings. It does not tell us the contents of this particular beaker, the share of each food in a diet or who performed each household task.

citations.locator: City of Kerma: house and courtyard paragraph

sections.title: An Egyptian findspot opens a further question
sections.text: The selected vessel has its own history: the museum dates it around 1802–1640 BCE and records its discovery in Abydos tomb 525. Kerma ceramics and Egyptian goods occur together in comparable graves. The museum proposes that some owners might have been traders from Kerma living in Egypt. That possibility makes an interesting research question, but the ceramic tradition does not identify an individual’s birthplace, language or occupation. The documented grave is firmer evidence than the proposed biography.

sections.title: Exchange and political relationships changed
sections.text: The Met’s regional chronology describes both trade and conflict between Kerma and Egypt. Imported objects entered elite tombs beside locally made equipment, while rulers negotiated alliances and contested control farther north. Later Egyptian campaigns changed the political setting. Keeping this sequence visible gives objects a changing institutional context instead of treating Nubia as a timeless source of distinctive pottery. Neither a traveled vessel nor a later Kushite royal name proves that the same government continued unchanged from Kerma to Taharqo’s much later reign.

deeperReading.title: Excavation changed the institutional explanation
deeperReading.text: Reisner initially interpreted the deffufa and adjacent structures as an Egyptian trading establishment. The mission account explains how later excavation identified the religious centre of an independent Nubian capital. This change matters: evidence of Egyptian goods does not make the city an Egyptian institution. Urban layout and local production can alter an explanation built too narrowly around imported objects.

citations.locator: La ville antique de Kerma: initial interpretation and renewed excavation

deeperReading.title: A courtyard is evidence at a particular scale
deeperReading.text: Kitchens and silos make provision visible within residential arrangements. They do not supply a household census or a complete administrative budget. The older project website also discusses later bread, beer and meat-offering workshops at Doukki Gel. Those belong to Napatan and Meroitic contexts: carrying their functions backward would replace Kerma’s evidence with a different period’s institutions.

citations.locator: City of Kerma: houses; Doukki Gel: Napatan/Meroitic annexes

deeperReading.title: Different clocks describe different investigations
deeperReading.text: The preserved case covers approximately 2050–1500 BCE. The project table separates Middle Kerma around 2050–1750 from Classic Kerma around 1750–1480; the Met uses a Classical convention around 1750–1550. These are published archaeological frames, not the beaker’s own date. Its catalogue range stays 1802–1640 BCE even where a style label and a phase boundary overlap imperfectly. No new chronological model has been run here.

deeperReading.title: Follow work without inventing its organization
deeperReading.text: A workshop near a temple suggests a relationship worth investigating. To explain control over supplies or skilled labor, seek dated storage evidence, material analyses and records that identify actual arrangements. The excavated proximity alone does not settle ownership or obligation. This distinction makes comparison with later palaces and royal funerary institutions productive while keeping their different dates and social settings intact.

evidenceReading.title: Separate an observation, a record and a proposal
evidenceReading.introduction: The following are editorial paraphrases and source interpretations, not ancient quotations.

items.label: The photographed surface
items.text: The photograph shows a dark upper area, red lower body and irregular transition band. The catalogue supplies a manufacturing explanation.
items.interpretation: Visible color is an observation; a firing method needs further evidence. The catalogue’s tentative coating explanation must remain tentative.

citations.locator: Description paragraphs1–2; actual local photograph inspected

items.label: A documented grave and a possible trader
items.text: Abydos tomb 525 is the recorded findspot. A trader from Kerma living in Egypt is the museum’s proposal for some comparable grave owners.
items.interpretation: An object’s location does not automatically identify the buried person. Additional contextual and biographical evidence would have to test the proposal.

items.label: Institutions reconstructed through excavation
items.text: The mission identifies temples, houses, administrative buildings and craft installations in the capital.
items.interpretation: Their spatial relationship informs an institutional account. It does not supply a payroll, production quota or proof of identical worker status.

familyActivity.title: Describe a surface; test a story
steps: Look at the supplied beaker photograph. Draw its outline and mark the dark area, red area and boundary between them. An adult can read the caption aloud.
Read the supplied findspot statement. Label your sketch with the recorded place, Abydos tomb 525, separately from what you can see.
Explain why the photograph and findspot do not tell you the buried person’s origin. Add one question that another record could help answer.
familyActivity.explanation: The task separates direct observation, catalogue context and a possible biography. No reproduction or real clay firing is required.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and author self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Selected account of Kerma manufacture, households and institutions, with a photograph-based family activity, original making guide, regional locators and a separate c.2500–1500 BCE reference. The bibliography details consultation and reuse limits.
limitations: The unchanged c.2050–1500 BCE case and the beaker’s c.1802–1640 BCE Abydos tomb 525 context remain distinct. Project Middle 2050–1750 and Classic 1750–1480 BCE conventions differ from the Met’s Classical 1750–1550 BCE; no endpoint is harmonized.

Consultation covers selected project/institutional web text, excluding excavation volumes, the original Abydos grave report, household census and full faunal/botanical datasets. Cereal-storage and copper papers remain inaccessible; snippets are not full-paper consultation.

Manufacture follows the catalogue; its glaze-like coating stays tentative. The photograph proves neither firing recipe nor contents. A possible trader remains an interpretation; birthplace, language, occupation, precise production place and travel route are unknown.

Workshop proximity proves neither royal monopoly, quotas, worker status nor gendered tasks. Household/food explanation remains selective. Later Napatan/Meroitic offering workshops are not projected backward. Newer Kerma-period Doukki Gel levels remain distinct from the older founding narrative. Comparison with Taharqo establishes no continuous government.

Project plan pixels were not inspected; figure reuse was not licensed or attempted. Met CC0 policy and the existing photograph were checked; original photograph/thumbnail bytes remain unchanged, without fresh source-image download or byte comparison.
Independent historian/community, family, screen-reader, device and physical-print acceptance remain open.

placeStudy.title: Kerma and Abydos: distinguish a capital from a findspot
placeStudy.description: Two regional references connect different kinds of evidence: a city with excavated craft and institutional spaces, and the area where this beaker was actually found. Coordinates alone do not identify a potter, owner, house or journey. The Nile and any route are not reconstructed in this locator diagram.

points.label: Kerma — regional capital setting
points.text: The project describes residential areas, craft activity and institutional buildings at Kerma. This broad reference near the inherited case anchor does not locate the selected vessel’s workshop. The beaker’s recorded grave context is elsewhere, at Abydos.

points.label: Abydos — recorded findspot region
points.text: The catalogue records Tomb 525 at Abydos. This minute-resolution regional point is not that grave’s surveyed position. A vessel’s style and its findspot do not by themselves identify the owner’s origin or reconstruct a journey between these points.
